item.title: Pineapple on pizza is an insult to our great Italian cuisine – and here’s why we secretly love it | Luca Cesari
item.description: Of course an Italian chef would rather be sacked than make this. Defending our food against such blasphemy makes us feel like better people Luca Cesari is a food historian and author of The History of Pizza You may have smiled at the news a few days ago: the Italian chef Davide Tamburella was sacked by a Brisbane restaurant after refusing to put pineapple on a pizza. Never mind that Queensland grows almost all of Australia’s pineapples. Tamburella would not give way to his customers or his boss, insisting that the combination was an insult to Italian culture. Strange as it may sound, he is not the first. In 2017, Maurizio Landi, a chef from Bologna, was sacked by a bistro near Lyon after resisting pressure to cook his pasta for longer and to serve spaghetti bolognese, a dish that does not exist in his home town. For anyone who doesn’t know, Bologna is the only city in the world where ragù is eaten solely with tagliatelle, and putting it on spaghetti borders on an outrage. Luca Cesari i

item.title: Albania’s restored stone houses throw open the doors to visitors
item.description: A project to convert the country’s traditional kulla houses into guesthouses offers a true flavour of ancient hospitality in a part of the country almost untouched by tourism Sunlight pours through a tiny stone window, causing the wooden floorboards to creak as they warm up. The sound of sheep’s bells filters in from a passing flock. The scent of baking bread mingles with smoke from the previous evening’s fire. I wake up feeling I’ve been transported back to another time – but in reality I’m in modern-day Albania. I’m staying in a kulla , one of the traditional stone tower houses that are found throughout northern Albania, Montenegro and North Macedonia. They once protected families during times of conflict and sheltered weary travellers on trade routes, before mostly falling into disrepair in the 20th century. A new long-distance trail developed by the Albanian Agritourism Association aims to return some of them to their former glory and give visitors a chance to discover a part of Al

item.title: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne’s legal thriller is so full of calamity it borders on Mr Bean-like farce
item.description: This slightly preposterous psychological drama – featuring Byrne and Meghann Fahy as sisters – is a show about trauma where everyone somehow looks astonishingly beautiful at all times At first glance, The Good Daughter (Thursday 12 November, 9pm, Sky Atlantic) should make you a little worried about Rose Byrne. Here is an actor not only at the top of her game, but quite frankly at the top of anybody’s. Her Apple TV show Platonic all but depends on her combination of emotional nuance and flawless slapstick to exist, and earlier this year she won a Golden Globe (and was nominated for an Oscar) for her wired, frayed lead performance in If I Had Legs I’d Kick You. In other words, Byrne should be able to make anything she wants. So it’s bizarre that, of all things, she has chosen this. The Good Daughter is a paperback thriller show. It’s one of those slightly preposterous programmes about trauma where everyone somehow manages to look astonishingly beautiful all the time. It’s David E Kelley

item.title: The Guide #268: Laptop twee is the gloriously awkward sound giving British music a new lease of life
item.description: In this week’s newsletter: From wonky electronic production to painfully earnest lyrics, a new wave of artists are embracing nostalgia, cute vibes and DIY pop If you’d told me back in January that one of my favourite tracks of 2026 would count noughties new rave outfit Hadouken! and goofy Kesha parodists The Midnight Beast among its influences, I would have looked at you skeptically, at the very least. I’m all for the nostalgic reappropriation of the most neglected and deeply uncool relics of pop music past, but these particular reference points would have seemed like a step too far. I would have been very wrong. The Ballad of St Nick’s Park by 300SkullsAndCounting (AKA Leamington Spa native Hal Hewetson) and his collaborator Jenny Sparks is one of the most unexpected and addictive songs I’ve heard in years. It’s also not as much of an outlier as it might initially seem; the pair’s album This Is Spa Town! is part of a new sound that was last year christened “laptop twee”. Other affilia

item.title: Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football
item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. item.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for roast beetroot with pickled raisins and blue cheese
item.description: Surprise yourself with the flavours in this roast beetroot spiked with pickled raisins and salty blue cheese It’s not uncommon for people to form negative relationships with certain vegetables as a consequence of only ever having had them boiled to disintegration, a blunt approach that’s unlikely to bring out the best in any of us. Beetroot, especially, are vastly improved by being roasted instead, because that way they cook gently in their own juices. Not only does this much improve their texture, but it concentrates their innate, earthy richness, rather than leaching out of them. Beetroot’s high level of natural sweetness makes it a perfect foil for sharp dressings and even sharper cheeses. Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London Continue reading...

item.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
item.description: Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions. Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.” Continue reading...

item.title: ‘My biggest fear was being shot down’: how an injured Ukrainian soldier was evacuated by drone
item.description: Artem Lytvyn tells of complex and risky rescue operation after he spent eight days stricken in Kharkiv’s ‘kill zone’ Artem Lytvyn was crossing a field when the bang happened. Up ahead was a tree line. Not far beyond that the Russian border. The 25-year-old Ukrainian soldier had spent five days trekking to a dangerous forward position in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Along the way he and six comrades dodged drones, and killed two Russians in a foxhole. A few hundred metres short of his destination, he trod on a mine. “I didn’t hear anything. It was a magnet type. My rifle set it off,” Lytvyn said. He applied two tourniquets to his shattered right leg and pulled off his combat boot. Fellow soldiers dragged him and another wounded platoon member, Siava, into bushes. The same blast ripped off Siava’s leg. He died two days later. Continue reading...

item.title: Yes, saunas are great – but have you heard of this amazing thing called a bath?

But if a trip to the spa seems like too much effort or money, then good news! An alternative could be waiting for you right behind your bathroom door: hot baths. Though washing habits have shifted towards showers in recent years, the majority of UK homes are still fitted with bathtubs. Not only is bathing less expensive than a sauna session; it may be more effective at lowering blood pressure and boosting the immune system, according to research from the University of Oregon . Continue reading...

item.title: Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option | Elisabeth Braw
item.description: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British te

item.title: Stabbed, jailed, reborn: the chef who lost his love of food – then regained it behind bars
item.description: Nathaniel Mortley dreamed of opening his own restaurant, but ended up in jail for drug offences. Now he’s out, and doing his best to make up for lost time At first he thought it was just a nasty punch, but Nathaniel Mortley soon realised he had been stabbed in the back. This was true in two senses. Figuratively, because he had been set up by a friend, and quite literally – since his back was gushing blood, as he saw reflected in the pub toilet mirror. It was 2010 and hours earlier, he had been at a street festival in south London. Life was looking up: he had just achieved good exam grades (14 GCSEs) and things were going well with his girlfriend. It was the final week before sixth form began and Mortley, who was 16 at the time, was due to continue his academic success, having signed up for five A-levels. Continue reading...

item.title: Edward Lucie-Smith obituary
item.description: Art historian, critic and poet who hosted ‘the Group’, a literary workshop of the 1950s and 60s The poet, art critic and historian Edward Lucie-Smith, who has died aged 93, was both prolific and polymathic. He wrote almost 100 full-length books, including studies of individual artists and large-scale historical surveys, among them The Male Nude: A Modern View (1985), Impressionist Women (1989) and Art and Civilization (1992). His suspicion of contemporary pieties did not lead him to any quick dismissal of contemporary work; rather, he remained permanently excited by the new, and keen to communicate what he saw in it. In an interview in 2017 , he gave his account of what he saw as the value of an art critic: “1. Pointing out what they think is good. 2. Saying why they think it’s good, in terms transparent enough for the audience they are addressing to understand.” His own work more than fulfilled this simple manifesto. Continue reading...

There was no guarantee, before the trial, that he would be found guilty; two more rape charges and one of attempted indecent assault ended in acquittal. The women who testified about what Brand did to them between 2004 and 2009 are owed a debt of gratitude by everyone who believes that sexual predators should pay a price for their crimes, even when they are celebrities. On Monday, Brand will receive what the judge said would be a “significant” jail sentence. The message sent by his rape conviction is particularly powerful. item.title: In jailing Joshua Wong, China is telling the world they'd crush every hope for democracy on its soil | Nathan Law
item.description: My friend was due to be released next January. Under draconian security laws, his sentence has been extended by 10 years Two years ago, I wrote in this newspaper about the lengthy imprisonment of my friend Joshua Wong, who I spent years campaigning alongside for the advancement of Hong Kong’s democracy. He was given an unjust sentence meant to keep him behind bars until January 2027. He was supposed to be released in a few months, when I hoped he would finally be able to reunite with his friends and family and embark on a new chapter. But this hope was misplaced. The end of the tunnel isn’t next year; it’s late 2036. By then, he will be 40. On Thursday, Joshua was sentenced to another 10 years under Hong Kong’s national security law for colluding with foreign forces. He is the only political prisoner who’s been convicted twice under the national security law. Her farewell UK concert at the London Palladium is approaching, and ahead of that she’ll join us to answer your questions. Born in Seattle in 1939, Collins’ career started out in the fertile folk scene of early 1960s New York, and became a close peer of the era’s great singer-songwriters. She recorded Joni Mitchell’s Both Sides, Now, even before Joni Mitchell did – reaching the US Top 10 with her version, which also won a Grammy – and also recorded early versions of songs by Leonard Cohen, Randy Newman and more. That’s who I am.” It’s an unnecessary clarification – at 61, he’s been nice on TV, as himself and in character, for most of our adult lives. We’re here to talk about his new six-parter, Bill’s Included, but his character in it, the eponymous Bill, is such a distillation of pure Rob Brydon that it’s (accidentally, he says) a celebration of his entire career. As the show opens, Bill has just been left by his wife, who’s run off with the gardener. At no point does he ever fire the guy – “I like him!” – but otherwise, his life is completely upended. I was lucky enough to come from a home full of books and when we joined my father out at sea for extended periods of time, my mother carried plenty of books for me to read. I remember sitting by the porthole in our cabin, looking out at the sea on a sunny day, the ship moving calmly through the waters. item.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

item.title: Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton review – climate urgency verges on panic, with moments of wonder too
item.description: The masterful Australian writer has become a kind of prophet – and his dramatic and moving new essay collection challenges us not to look away Tim Winton has been working his themes for almost 50 years in a palimpsest of 32 books: family, manhood, land and ocean; what it is to be human and Australian; intimate pleasures and anxieties that feed his fiction. The distinctive quality of his new collection of memoir and essays, Songs from the Firefront, is urgency verging on panic. He’s an elder in his 60s, with limited time to get his messages across before we all go up in flames. Living on the western edge of Australia, Winton has been an eloquent climate-change activist for decades . He has fought, with tenuous success, to protect Ningaloo Reef. He entrances us with Scheherazade stories that blend crystalline nature writing and terrifying facts. The loss has accelerated now, he says, and the danger is immediate. Songs from the Firefront by Tim Winton is out now through Hamish Hamilton/Pe

item.title: My childhood was one of survival and resilience. How can I model a joyful life for my kids? | Leading questions
item.description: Start with the feeling, not the activities, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith . Making more room for enjoyment is also making more room for your actual self Read more Leading questions I’m a child of first-generation immigrants and have always carried a story of survival and resilience. My parents were part of a “lost generation” who sacrificed a lot to put us all through university . There was a very defined path for success, some of which I followed and some not. I married outside of race; I made work choices for financial stability . I don’t know how to enjoy things that other people seem to. Hobbies, travelling, home renovations … I look at those like “what is the point?” I want to say it’s because my upbringing was not full of leisure activities; my parents only allowed us to focus on academic topics. Now that I’m a mother though, I wonder how I can role model some of this “living well for its own sake” for my children. It’s hard to find simple joys actually joyful. Gro

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye? item.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution

That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and other parts of Southeast Asia.

item.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

item.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
item.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

item.title: Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
item.description: John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic. The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points. Continue reading...

The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules. item.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

item.description: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

item.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
item.description: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge.

item.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
item.description: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

item.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
item.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

item.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
item.description: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4 The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks.

item.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03505-1 For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat.

item.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?

item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03413-4 Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.

item.title: Infrared image detectors grown directly on read-out chips
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03420-5 A film of lead sulfide — an infrared-sensitive semiconductor — has been grown directly on a circuit that can read out the material’s electrical signal through an approach called monolithic in situ integration. This brings material growth and electronic integration together into a single step. The resulting image sensor shows high sensitivity for infrared wavelengths.

item.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8 A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.

item.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11133-y Recent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.

item.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10956-z Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

item.title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11225-9 A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.

item.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11209-9 In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

item.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6 AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

item.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11148-5 The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

item.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11238-4 Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

item.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11177-0 Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11212-0 A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.

item.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11226-8 Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

item.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11245-5 Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

item.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11200-4 Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.

item.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11198-9 Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.

item.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11224-w Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

item.title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5 A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

item.title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11248-2 Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

item.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9 Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

item.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11236-6 Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain.

item.title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5 Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

item.title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe<sub>2</sub>
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11274-0 Twist-angle-dependent studies of moiré bilayer MoTe2 reveal a transition from fractional topological states to correlated insulators and superconductivity, linking topology, symmetry breaking and magnetism in moiré quantum materials.

item.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11210-2 structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families.

item.title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11243-7 Viral–bacterial synergy accelerates algal bloom collapse by enhancing virus-induced mortality, driven by Alteromonas chemoattraction and co-infection, revealing a previously unrecognized mortality agent that influences oceanic carbon cycling .

item.title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11187-y The genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China are traced using representative cultivars, demonstrating how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

item.title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11220-0 Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation.

item.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11234-8 A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

item.title: ‘The nipple touch of doom’: what is sad nipple syndrome and what causes it?
item.description: People everywhere are searching for the reason behind their sudden bursts of anguish or homesickness Women: was your autoimmune condition misdiagnosed? Some say it feels like a sudden burst of anguish ; others liken it more to homesickness. The sudden onset of a sinking, upsetting feeling due to nipple stimulation is anecdotally known as Sad Nipple Syndrome (SNS) , and for Sandra, it can be triggered by something as commonplace as putting on a shirt. “I was probably a child when I first noticed: ‘Why does touching my nipple make me sad?’” says the 28-year-old. The sensation seemed to happen at random, and without the words to describe it, she kept it a secret. It wasn’t until college that she worked up the courage to Google it. “I realized I wasn’t crazy,” she says. Continue reading...

item.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.

Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
